name: Software engineer
summary: Software engineer interviews usually combine coding (solving a problem out loud, often in a shared editor), computer science fundamentals and a discussion of your projects. For experienced roles, many companies add a system design round and ask how you've handled production issues and trade-offs; for freshers, expect more on data structures, OOP and final-year or internship work.
rounds: Online coding test or recruiter screen (for campus hiring, often an aptitude and coding test)
One or two coding interviews: solve a problem out loud and discuss its complexity
Computer science fundamentals: data structures, OOP, databases, operating systems and networks
System design or low-level design round (mostly for experienced roles)
Hiring manager or behavioural round on projects, teamwork and ownership
looks_for: Clarifying the problem before writing code, and thinking out loud
Choosing a data structure for a reason and stating time and space complexity
Working, readable code, tested against edge cases you name yourself
Depth on your own projects: what you built, why, and what you'd change
Sensible design trade-offs: simplicity, scale, cost and failure

questions.text: Tell me about the hardest bug you've fixed. How did you track it down?
covers: The symptom and why it was hard to reproduce
How you narrowed it down: logs, a debugger, comparing a working and a broken version
The root cause, the fix, and the test you added so it couldn't return

questions.text: Describe a time you disagreed with a teammate about how to build something.
covers: Both approaches, described fairly
How you compared them: data, a quick prototype, a review with others
What was decided and how you worked together afterwards

questions.text: Tell me about a time code you wrote caused a problem for users. What did you do?
covers: What broke, who was affected, and how you found out
How you fixed or rolled back quickly and kept people informed
What you changed in testing or review afterwards

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to get productive in an unfamiliar codebase quickly.
covers: How you found your way around: entry points, running it locally, asking the right people
A small first change you made to learn safely
What you delivered and how long it took

questions.text: Walk me through the project you're proudest of. What did you build yourself, and what would you change now?
covers: The problem and who it was for, in a sentence
Your own part, the stack, and one hard technical decision
What you'd redo with what you know now

questions.text: Explain the difference between a process and a thread, and when you'd use more than one thread.
covers: Processes have separate memory; threads share memory within a process
Why threads help: waiting on input and output, using several cores
The cost: race conditions, locks and deadlocks, with an example

questions.text: How does a hash map work underneath, and when would you choose a different structure?
covers: Hashing a key to a bucket, and how collisions are handled
Constant-time lookups on average, and what makes them slower
When an ordered structure such as a balanced tree or a sorted array is the better fit

questions.text: Explain encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism using an example from code you've written.
covers: Each idea in plain words, plus abstraction
An example from your own project rather than a textbook animal or shape
When composition is a better choice than inheritance

questions.text: What happens, step by step, when you type a web address into a browser and press Enter?
covers: A DNS lookup, then a TCP connection and a TLS handshake for HTTPS
The HTTP request, the server's response and the browser rendering the page
Where caching happens along the way

questions.text: Your solution works but is too slow for large inputs. How do you go about speeding it up?
covers: Finding the repeated work with a complexity estimate rather than guessing
Typical fixes: a better data structure, sorting first, caching results, avoiding nested loops
Checking the faster version still handles the edge cases

questions.text: Talk me through how you'd design a service that lets people share a file through a link that expires.
covers: Requirements first: file sizes, how long links last, who can open them, rough traffic
Files in object storage, link details in a database
Hard-to-guess links, expiry, cleaning up old files, and what happens under heavy load

questions.text: How would you design the database tables for an app where students enrol in courses? Which indexes would you add?
covers: Tables for students, courses and enrolments, with keys linking them
Why a many-to-many relationship needs its own table, and normalisation in plain words
Indexes for the most common lookups, and their cost on writes

questions.text: Your service became slow in production right after yesterday's release. How do you investigate?
covers: Confirming the impact with metrics and checking exactly what changed in the release
Narrowing it down: database queries, calls to other services, memory or CPU limits
Rolling back if users are affected, then finding the root cause

questions.text: How do you decide what to test, and what's the difference between unit and integration tests?
covers: Unit tests check one piece in isolation; integration tests check pieces working together
Testing behaviour and edge cases rather than chasing a coverage number
An example of a test that caught a bug for you

questions.text: What are Git branches and pull requests for, and how do you resolve a merge conflict?
covers: Branches let work happen in parallel without breaking the main line
Pull requests for review and automated checks before merging
Resolving a conflict by understanding both changes, not just picking one side

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and why you want to work as a software engineer.
covers: Your education or current role in a sentence or two
One or two projects or results that show how you build things
Why this kind of work, and why this team, briefly

questions.text: Why do you want to join us? What do you know about our product and the engineering behind it?
covers: Something specific about the product, its users or its technical challenges
How your skills or interests match the work the team does
What you hope to learn or own in your first year

tips: Talk while you code: say your approach and its complexity before typing, so the interviewer can steer you early.
Before saying you're done, run your code by hand on a small example and one edge case: empty input, one element, duplicates.
Know every line of the projects on your resume; interviewers often pick one and ask why you built it that way.
In design rounds, spend the first few minutes on requirements and rough scale; they shape every choice after.
If you're stuck, say what you're trying and ask a focused question; silence is harder to help than a wrong idea.
Prepare stories about a bug, a disagreement and a deadline; behavioural questions come up in technical loops too.
